prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Volcanic ash builds fertile soil, drawing farmers despite the danger of eruptions.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains the fertility-versus-danger trade-off that keeps farmers near volcanoes.

choices.text: Potassium is the single mineral that crops need in order to grow well.
choices.rationale: It names potassium and phosphorus, not a single required mineral.

choices.text: Farming is effectively impossible anywhere within reach of a volcano.
choices.rationale: The passage says many people do farm there.

choices.text: Volcanoes pose essentially no danger to the farms and villages that sit on their slopes.
choices.rationale: The passage notes a real danger, so volcanoes are not harmless.

explanation: The passage balances the benefit of fertile soil against eruption risk.

stimulus.title: Gifts of the Volcano
stimulus.text: It seems strange that people would farm in the shadow of a volcano, but many do, and for good reason. When a volcano erupts, it scatters ash rich in minerals such as potassium and phosphorus. Over years, this ash breaks down into some of the most fertile soil on Earth. Crops planted in it can grow unusually well, which is why slopes near certain volcanoes are crowded with farms and villages. The bargain is uneasy: the same mountain that feeds the fields can also threaten them. Farmers weigh the steady gift of rich soil against the rare but real danger overhead, and generation after generation, many choose to stay.

prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: The tardigrade can survive only in the vacuum and radiation of outer space.
choices.rationale: Space is one extreme it can survive, not its home.

choices.text: The tardigrade endures extreme conditions by drying into a protected, revivable state.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage centers on how the tardigrade endures extremes by drying out.

choices.text: The tardigrade is the smallest animal that scientists have ever discovered anywhere on Earth.
choices.rationale: The passage compares its size to salt but never calls it the smallest animal.

choices.text: Scientists have now fully explained exactly how the tardigrade protects its cells.
choices.rationale: The text says scientists are 'still untangling' the mechanism.

explanation: The passage's focus is the dehydration survival strategy and its partial explanation.

stimulus.title: The Survivor
stimulus.text: Smaller than a grain of salt, the tardigrade looks almost comical, plodding on eight stubby legs. Its talent, however, is anything but ordinary. When its surroundings dry out, the creature expels most of its water and curls into a husk called a tun. In this state it can endure boiling heat, the vacuum of space, and doses of radiation that would kill nearly any other animal. Years later, a single drop of water can revive it. Scientists are still untangling how the tardigrade protects its cells, but one clue is a special set of proteins that seem to harden into glass, cradling delicate structures until water returns.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Human accents are largely caused by people imitating nearby birdsong.
choices.rationale: The human-accent comparison is an analogy, not a cause.

choices.text: Sparrows learn local song dialects that vary by place and shift across generations.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains learned, place-based dialects that change over generations.

choices.text: Every white-crowned sparrow sings exactly the same unchanging song wherever it lives.
choices.rationale: The passage stresses variation, not sameness.

choices.text: Sparrows are born already knowing the full song they will sing as adults.
choices.rationale: Birds must learn the song; they are not born knowing it.

explanation: The passage's through-line is learned, drifting song dialects.

stimulus.title: Songs With Accents
stimulus.text: A white-crowned sparrow raised near San Francisco does not sing quite like one raised a hundred miles north. The basic melody is the same, but small flourishes differ from place to place, forming what biologists call song dialects. Young sparrows learn these dialects by listening to adult males during a brief window in their first months. A bird that hears no song in that window grows up to sing a thin, simplified tune. The dialects can drift over generations, much as human accents do, so a recording made decades ago may sound subtly foreign to the birds singing in the same meadow today.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Ancient people were unable to count sheep or coins without using zero.
choices.rationale: The passage says people counted sheep and coins easily without zero.

choices.text: Treating zero as a true number transformed how people could write and calculate.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage shows how recognizing zero as a number reshaped writing and calculation.

choices.text: Mathematicians decided that zero should be removed entirely from written calculations.
choices.rationale: Mathematicians embraced zero, rather than removing it.

choices.text: Zero was always understood as an ordinary number throughout all of history.
choices.rationale: The passage says zero was long absent and unsettling, not always understood.

explanation: The passage's point is that accepting zero as a number transformed mathematics.

stimulus.title: The Number That Was Nothing
stimulus.text: For much of history, there was no symbol for nothing. People counted sheep and coins easily enough, but the idea of writing down an empty amount seemed pointless, even unsettling. The breakthrough came when mathematicians treated zero not as the absence of a number but as a number in its own right, one that could be added, subtracted, and used to hold a place in larger figures. With zero, the difference between 5 and 50 could be written clearly, and long calculations grew far simpler. A concept that once felt like a riddle became the quiet hinge on which much of modern mathematics turns.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Plastic disappears completely and harmlessly once sunlight has acted on it.
choices.rationale: It says plastic fragments rather than vanishes.

choices.text: Microplastics can be filtered out of the open ocean cheaply and quite easily.
choices.rationale: The passage says filtering is nearly impossible.

choices.text: Plastic breaks into tiny, far-spread particles that resist removal, so prevention is best.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage describes the spread and persistence of microplastics and favors prevention.

choices.text: Scientists have firmly proven that microplastics pose no danger whatsoever to human health.
choices.rationale: It says health effects are not yet clear.

explanation: The passage links persistence and spread to a prevention-first conclusion.

stimulus.title: Small Pieces, Wide Reach
stimulus.text: Plastic does not simply vanish. Exposed to sunlight and waves, a bottle or bag breaks into ever-smaller fragments until the pieces are too tiny to see. These microplastics have turned up in river water, in Arctic ice, and even in the bodies of fish and birds. Because the particles are so small, filtering them out of the ocean is nearly impossible. Researchers caution that the full effects on health are not yet clear, and they warn against easy conclusions. What is clear is that the cheapest fix is also the simplest: keeping plastic out of the environment in the first place, before it can shatter into pieces no net can catch.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Rivers carry only clear water and never any soil from distant hills.
choices.rationale: The passage says rivers carry soil, not only water.

choices.text: Dams reliably help deltas grow larger by holding back excess water.
choices.rationale: Dams starve deltas by trapping sediment, not helping them grow.

choices.text: A delta is built by river sediment and shrinks when that supply is cut off.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains deltas as sediment-built land that erodes when the supply is trapped.

choices.text: Deltas are permanent landforms that never change once they have formed.
choices.rationale: The passage stresses deltas are a constantly rebuilt balance, not permanent.

explanation: The passage shows deltas as sediment-dependent land that retreats when starved of mud.

stimulus.title: Land Made of Mud
stimulus.text: A great river carries more than water; it carries soil, scoured from distant hills and ground into fine particles. Where the river finally slows and meets the sea, it can no longer hold this load, and the sediment settles out, building flat new land called a delta. Over centuries a delta can grow seaward, fanning into a maze of channels and islands. But the process depends on a steady supply of mud. When dams upstream trap that sediment, the delta is starved; waves carry off more land than the river replaces, and the coastline begins to retreat. What looks like permanent ground is, in truth, a balance constantly being rebuilt.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: People universally welcomed standard time the moment it was first proposed.
choices.rationale: The passage says people grumbled at first before accepting the change.

choices.text: Standard time zones existed long before any railroads were ever built.
choices.rationale: Time zones came in response to railroads, not before them.

choices.text: Towns before railroads all happened to keep exactly the same time as one another by chance.
choices.rationale: The passage says each town kept its own time, not the same time.

choices.text: Railroads drove the shift from local sun time to shared, standardized time zones.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains how railway schedules forced a move to shared time zones.

explanation: The passage's point is that railroads pushed local time into standardized zones.

stimulus.title: When Noon Moved
stimulus.text: Before railroads, every town kept its own time, set by the sun overhead at noon. A traveler crossing the country adjusted a watch town by town, and no one minded a few minutes' difference. Railroads made the patchwork intolerable. Trains ran on schedules, and a schedule means nothing if each station defines noon differently; a missed connection could be a matter of life and death. So the railways carved the land into broad zones, each agreeing to share a single time. People grumbled at first about clocks that no longer matched the sun, but the convenience won out. The hour on the wall had become a public agreement rather than a private reading of the sky.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: The bicycle evolved through gradual improvements into a popular means of free travel.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage traces stepwise improvements leading to the bicycle's popularity and freedom of movement.

choices.text: Early bicycles still depended on a horse in order to move from place to place.
choices.rationale: The passage says it needed no horse.

choices.text: Working foot pedals were a built-in part of the very first bicycle design.
choices.rationale: The earliest version had no pedals.

choices.text: The very first bicycle was an immediate and widely celebrated success with the public.
choices.rationale: The first version was mocked and faded, not an immediate success.

explanation: The passage's arc is incremental improvement culminating in widespread, independent travel.

stimulus.title: The Machine That Walked
stimulus.text: The earliest ancestor of the bicycle had no pedals at all. Built in 1817, it was a wooden frame on two wheels that a rider straddled and pushed along with the feet, like walking while seated. People mocked it, and rutted roads made it impractical, so it soon faded. Decades passed before inventors added pedals, then a chain, then air-filled tires that smoothed the ride. Each change drew new riders, and by the 1890s the bicycle had become a craze. It offered something rare for the time: cheap, independent travel that needed no horse and no rails. For many people, especially those long denied easy movement, the machine quietly widened the boundaries of daily life.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Only scholars who lived in the city itself were ever allowed to use the library's scrolls.
choices.rationale: Scholars came from distant lands.

choices.text: The library was destroyed in a single, well-documented, and sudden great fire.
choices.rationale: The passage says the single-fire story oversimplifies a slow decline.

choices.text: The library, as a matter of policy, refused to copy any scroll brought to it.
choices.rationale: The library actively copied scrolls.

choices.text: The library pursued a sweeping goal of universal knowledge whose ideal outlived it.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage stresses the ambition of universal collection and the lasting power of that idea.

explanation: The passage's emphasis is the ambitious ideal and its endurance, not a single dramatic end.

stimulus.title: A House for Every Book
stimulus.text: The ancient library at Alexandria aimed at something audacious: to gather a copy of every book in the world. Ships docking at the harbor were searched, and any scrolls aboard were copied; sometimes the library kept the original and returned the copy. Scholars from distant lands came to read, argue, and write, and the collection may have held hundreds of thousands of scrolls. We know less than we would like about how the library declined, and popular stories of a single great fire oversimplify a slow loss across centuries. Still, the idea behind it endured. The dream of one place that holds all knowledge has reappeared, in new forms, ever since.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Modern forecasting completely discarded every part of the older tradition of weather watching.
choices.rationale: The passage says modern forecasting absorbed, not discarded, the best parts.

choices.text: Folk weather knowledge was entirely accurate and never mistaken in any case.
choices.rationale: The passage says much folk knowledge was unreliable.

choices.text: Farmers ignored the sky and the land when trying to predict the weather.
choices.rationale: The passage shows farmers read the sky and land closely.

choices.text: Folk weather signs mixed superstition with genuine insight that modern forecasting absorbed.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage says folk signs blended superstition and real wisdom, the best of which forecasting absorbed.

explanation: The passage balances the flaws and genuine insight of folk weather signs.

stimulus.title: Reading the Weather Before Radio
stimulus.text: Long before satellites mapped storms from orbit, farmers learned to read the sky and the land for signs of coming weather. A ring of haze around the moon, the smell of soil before rain, the behavior of swallows flying low: such clues were gathered into almanacs and passed down through families. Much of this folk knowledge was unreliable, mixing keen observation with superstition. Yet some of it held real wisdom, since the conditions that produce a hazy moon truly can precede rain. Modern forecasting has not so much replaced this older watching as absorbed its best parts, trading the rooster's crow for the radar's sweep.

prompt: The primary purpose of the text is to

choices.text: describe the technical steps involved in baking a loaf of bread from scratch
choices.rationale: Only a few steps are mentioned, and they serve the story rather than instruct.

choices.text: recount how a brief remark from a mentor taught the narrator a lesson about patience
choices.rationale: Correct. The text builds to Mrs. Delgado's remark and the narrator's lasting lesson about not rushing.

choices.text: explain why the narrator eventually chose a career as a professional baker
choices.rationale: Nothing indicates the narrator became a baker.

choices.text: argue that practical summer jobs teach adolescents far more than formal schooling ever can
choices.rationale: The narrator compares the remark favorably with school but makes no general argument about jobs.

explanation: The narrative exists to deliver the lesson 'Bread is not' in a hurry and its effect on the narrator.

stimulus.title: Proof
stimulus.text: The summer I was sixteen, I worked the four a.m. shift at Delgado's, mostly because nobody else would. Mrs. Delgado did not believe in teaching; she believed in watching. For two weeks I shaped loaves beside her while she said nothing, and for two weeks my loaves came out of the oven squat and sullen, like they resented being made. Then one morning she pressed a finger into my dough, frowned, and said, 'You are in a hurry. Bread is not.' That was all. I slowed down. I let the dough rest in the proof box until it had nearly doubled, instead of until I got bored. The loaf that came out that day was not perfect, but it rose. I have thought about that sentence more often than anything I learned in school, mostly when I am about to rush something that will not be rushed.

prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Staying awake for longer stretches reliably improves a person's memory of new material.
choices.rationale: The experiment shows the opposite of this claim.

choices.text: The brain does essentially nothing of value during the hours a person sleeps.
choices.rationale: The passage argues the brain is busy during sleep.

choices.text: The more hours a person sleeps each night, the better that person performs.
choices.rationale: The passage explicitly rejects 'more is always better.'

choices.text: Sleep is an active process that supports memory and brain upkeep, in the right amount.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage presents sleep as active and beneficial within an optimal range.

explanation: The passage's balanced claim is that sleep actively helps the brain, but only in adequate amounts.

stimulus.title: The Night Shift of the Brain
stimulus.text: Sleep can look like idleness, but the brain is busy. During deep sleep, waves of electrical activity sweep across the cortex, and researchers think these waves help move the day's memories into longer-term storage. In one line of experiments, students who slept after studying a list of words remembered more of them than students who stayed awake the same number of hours. Sleep may also clear away molecular waste that builds up while we are awake. None of this means more sleep is always better; the relationship appears to follow a curve, with both too little and too much linked to poorer performance. What the brain seems to need is enough, at the right times.

prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.text: Polar snow melts completely each summer before the next winter's snowfall.
choices.rationale: The passage says winter snow does not entirely melt.

choices.text: Ice cores preserve ancient air in layered bubbles that record past atmospheres.
choices.rationale: Correct. The passage explains how layered ice traps and dates ancient air.

choices.text: Drilling into ice destroys the trapped bubbles before they can be studied.
choices.rationale: The passage describes analyzing the bubbles, not destroying them.

choices.text: Ice cores are useful only for measuring the present-day composition of air.
choices.rationale: Cores let researchers study ancient, not just present, air.

explanation: The passage centers on ice cores as a layered record of past atmospheres.

stimulus.title: Bubbles of Old Air
stimulus.text: Each winter's snowfall on a polar ice sheet does not entirely melt; it packs down, traps tiny pockets of air, and slowly turns to ice. Layer settles on layer, year after year, so that drilling deep into the ice is a way of drilling back through time. Trapped in those bubbles is a sample of the very atmosphere that existed when the snow fell, including the gases it carried. By analyzing cores pulled from kilometers down, researchers can compare today's air with the air of tens of thousands of years ago. The ice keeps no diary of dates, yet its layers, counted carefully, let scientists assign an age to each whisper of ancient air.

prompt: Which choice best describes what happens in the text?

choices.text: A chess coach interrupts a tournament match to advise his student on managing her remaining time.
choices.rationale: The coach's voice is remembered, not present.

choices.text: A chess player loses her knight through carelessness and realizes too late that the game is lost.
choices.rationale: The knight is given up deliberately, as part of a plan.

choices.text: Two chess players agree to a draw after both run short of time in a long and evenly matched game.
choices.rationale: No draw occurs.

choices.text: Under time pressure, a chess player narrows her focus and commits to a sacrifice that unsettles her opponent.
choices.rationale: Correct. Priya applies her coach's advice, finds a path requiring the knight, and the boy finally looks up.

explanation: The scene turns on Priya's focused decision and its effect on her opponent.

stimulus.title: Forty Moves
stimulus.text: By the thirtieth move, Priya had stopped seeing the pieces as pieces. The knight on the rim was a trapped thing with one way out; the pawn on the sixth rank was a promise she had made twenty moves earlier and now had to keep. Across the table her opponent, a boy in a sweatshirt who had not looked up once, took her bishop with an unhurried hand and pressed the clock. Nine minutes left for her, fourteen for him. Her coach's voice surfaced: when you are behind on time, do not think faster; think about fewer things. She let the whole board blur except for the pawn and the two squares in front of it. There was a path. It required giving up the knight, which her hand did not want to do, and she noticed, with something like amusement, that her hand had opinions. She moved the knight anyway. The boy looked up.

prompt: Which choice best describes the overall impression the letter conveys?

choices.text: The writer believes the captain deceived the travelers and intends to expose his dishonesty.
choices.rationale: He treats the captain's lateness wryly, not as deception to be exposed.

choices.text: The writer is thrilled by the beauty of the landscape and eager for his family to join him there soon.
choices.rationale: He says the country is 'nothing like the engravings' and describes it unflatteringly.

choices.text: The writer regrets leaving home and plans to return to his family as soon as he possibly can.
choices.rationale: He expresses no plan to return.

choices.text: The writer is disappointed by the camp but finds small compensations in the experience.
choices.rationale: Correct. Thomas catalogs disappointments but values the lesson about finding water.

explanation: The letter balances complaint with a note of something gained.

stimulus.title: A Letter from the Camp
stimulus.text: Dear Margaret, You will forgive the hand; I am writing on the lid of a trunk by the light of a lamp that smokes. We reached the river camp on Tuesday, two days later than the captain promised and a full week later than Father feared, which puts the truth, as usual, somewhere between hope and worry. The country here is nothing like the engravings. The hills are brown and lie about in heaps, and the river is the color of weak coffee. I had expected to be lonely and find instead that I am never alone, which is worse. There are forty of us in a space meant for twenty. Still, this morning a boy no older than you showed me how to find water by watching where the birds go at dusk, and I thought: here is something I would not have learned at home. Tell Mother I am eating. It is nearly true. Your brother, Thomas.

prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Ines resents the lighthouse and performs her father's duties only because no one else in the family is willing.
choices.rationale: The text says she does not love the lighthouse 'exactly,' but it describes attachment, not resentment, and no other family members appear.

choices.text: Ines dreams of leaving the lighthouse so that she can finally speak with the sailors whose ships pass at night.
choices.rationale: She values the imagined contact with sailors; nothing suggests she wants to leave.

choices.text: Ines takes over her ill father's duties and finds meaning in the beam's silent message to distant sailors.
choices.rationale: Correct. The text follows Ines doing her father's work and locates her feeling in the beam reaching unseen sailors.

choices.text: Ines has grown so skilled at tending the lamp that she now keeps the log far more carefully than her father ever did.
choices.rationale: Her script is described as 'looser' than her father's careful hand, so she is not more careful than he was.

explanation: The passage centers on Ines's quiet stewardship of the light and the one-word 'conversation' it lets her have.

stimulus.title: The Lamp Room
stimulus.text: Every evening at dusk, Ines climbed the one hundred and twelve iron steps to the lamp room, counting them under her breath as her father had taught her. He was ill that winter, and the keeper's log, which he had kept in his cramped, careful hand for twenty years, now bore her looser script. She trimmed the wick, polished the great lens until her own face swam in it, and set the clockwork turning. Below, the sea worried at the rocks. Ines did not love the lighthouse, exactly; she loved the moment when the beam first swung out across the water and she imagined a ship's mate, miles off, lifting his head. It was the only conversation she had ever had with strangers, and it consisted of a single word, repeated all night: here.

prompt: Which choice best describes the text's central concern?

choices.text: A woman has decided to leave her family permanently in order to pursue a career in music.
choices.rationale: She 'had not yet decided whether she would get on.'

choices.text: A woman stands between the life she has and an opportunity she had set aside.
choices.rationale: Correct. The letter from her past and her indecision on the platform frame the choice.

choices.text: A woman is annoyed that her town has never bothered to repair the station's unreliable clock.
choices.rationale: The clock is atmosphere, not her concern.

choices.text: A woman is traveling to the city to care for an ailing cousin for a period of two weeks.
choices.rationale: The cousin is a cover story; 'the fortnight did not' exist.

explanation: The scene is a woman poised between two lives.

stimulus.title: The Eleven-Forty
stimulus.text: The station at Harwell had two platforms and one clock, and the clock was wrong, which everyone in town knew and no one corrected. Mrs. Abernathy stood under it in her good coat with a hatbox at her feet. She had told her sister she was going to visit a cousin in the city for a fortnight. The cousin existed; the fortnight did not. In her handbag, beneath the gloves, was a letter from a music conservatory addressed to a Miss E. Abernathy, which she had not been for twelve years, and which she had opened at the kitchen table that morning while the kettle screamed and nobody came to take it off. The eleven-forty was late. It was always late, by exactly the amount the clock was wrong, so that it arrived, in a manner of speaking, on time. She picked up the hatbox when she heard it. She had not yet decided whether she would get on.

prompt: Which choice best states the author's main argument?

choices.text: Rest should be understood primarily as an investment that yields returns in the quality of later work.
choices.rationale: This is the view the author criticizes.

choices.text: Unstructured time is valuable in itself and is also the condition for the insight that productivity culture wants.
choices.rationale: Correct. The author defends time 'not for anything' and notes that insight comes from it anyway.

choices.text: People should work fewer hours so that they have more time to rest and recover from their demanding jobs.
choices.rationale: The author says 'I do not propose that anyone work less.'

choices.text: Tracking habits and optimizing schedules are the most effective ways of solving stubborn intellectual problems quickly.
choices.rationale: The author says problems come loose away from the desk.

explanation: Idle time is defended both for its own sake and for what it yields.

stimulus.title: In Defense of Doing Nothing
stimulus.text: We have made an idol of productivity. Every hour is to be optimized, every habit tracked, every pause justified as 'recharging' for the work to come. Even rest is permitted only as an investment. I want to argue for something less respectable: time that is not for anything. The case is not sentimental. Most people can name the moment a stubborn problem came loose, and it was rarely at the desk. It was in the shower, on a walk, in the dull middle of a long drive. The mind does its deepest sorting when it is left alone, and it cannot be left alone on a schedule. A culture that fills every gap does not merely tire its members; it starves the very faculty it claims to prize. I do not propose that anyone work less. I propose that when the work is done, we stop pretending that the hours afterward owe us a return. Some of them will pay anyway. That is not why they are worth having.

prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The narrator's master was so cautious in his work that he failed to complete most of the charts the Admiralty had commissioned from him.
choices.rationale: Nothing suggests Hallam failed to complete charts.

choices.text: The narrator came to believe that a map with gaps is useless to sailors and should never be issued by the Admiralty.
choices.rationale: The narrator values gaps, not rejects them.

choices.text: A northern voyage failed to survey a stretch of coast because of nine days of fog, forcing the Admiralty to send a second expedition.
choices.rationale: No second expedition is mentioned; the fog is the occasion, not the subject.

choices.text: A mapmaker's refusal to invent a coastline taught the narrator that honesty about ignorance outweighs a finished look.
choices.rationale: Correct. Hallam leaves the gap, and the narrator comes to see gaps as 'the most honest lines.'

explanation: Honesty about what is unknown is the lesson.

stimulus.title: The Unfinished Coast
stimulus.text: My master, Mr. Hallam, had drawn maps for the Admiralty for thirty years, and in all that time, he told me, he had never once drawn a line he had not been given reason to believe. I was nineteen and thought this a modest ambition. It was my task that winter to copy the surveys sent back from the northern voyage, and I came to a stretch of coast where the ship's log simply stopped: fog for nine days, then open sea. The chart before me showed a gap. I proposed to close it with a gentle curve, as any sensible coast would run. Mr. Hallam took the pen from my hand. 'A sailor who trusts that curve,' he said, 'will put his ship on rocks we have not seen, and he will do it in the dark, and he will do it because you were tidy.' He left the gap. I have since drawn a great many maps, and some of them have gaps, and I have come to think of the gaps as the most honest lines on them.

prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Keeping a written record of weekly failures is the most reliable way to become wiser over the course of a lifetime.
choices.rationale: The original list made the author miserable, not wiser.

choices.text: Separating what one controls from what one does not makes self-assessment more honest and less painful.
choices.rationale: Correct. The author adopts the philosophers' line and finds the resulting list truer and more bearable.

choices.text: The ancient philosophers were wrong to claim that events outside our control are of little importance to our lives.
choices.rationale: The text says the philosophers did not call external events unimportant.

choices.text: Judging oneself by the moods of colleagues and the outcomes of distant events is a sign of unusual conscientiousness.
choices.rationale: The author presents this habit as a mistake, not a virtue.

explanation: The essay's arc is from a self-punishing list to one limited to what is 'ours.'

stimulus.title: What Is Ours
stimulus.text: I used to keep a list of things that had gone wrong that week, with the idea that reviewing it would make me wiser. It made me miserable instead, and I eventually understood why. Most of the items were not mine. The weather, a colleague's mood, the outcome of a vote in a city I had never visited: I had been grading myself on events in which I had no vote. An ancient school of philosophers drew a line that I have since found useful. On one side are the things within our power—our judgments, our efforts, our intentions. On the other side is everything else. They did not say that the second category is unimportant, only that it is not ours, and that confusing the two is the chief source of unhappiness. I still keep a list. It is shorter now, and every item on it is something I actually did, or failed to do. On bad weeks it is a harder list to read. On good weeks it is the only one that counts.
